newsitem.title: PERU: Rain halts search for hundreds under Peru mudslide.
newsitem.headline: Rain halts search for hundreds under Peru mudslide.

text.p: Torrential rain and the risk of further landslips prevented rescuers from searching on Friday for the bodies of up to 300 peasants entombed under a mudslide in the Andes of southeastern Peru.
The rain also held up planes trying to fly in emergency aid to the zone, where thousands have been left homeless.
Only 43 bodies have been retrieved from the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra, which were buried by a torrent of mud, dirt and rocks before dawn on Tuesday.
Distraught relatives and the few survivors waited for more bodies to be dug up, but soldiers and volunteers using sniffer dogs were not hopeful.
"It is impossible to contine the rescue today," said Marco Suarez, an official from the nearby Tamburco community. "I think the people trapped under the mud are already very deep."
All nearby villages were being evacuated under army supervision, with inhabitants taking refuge in schools, churches and buildings of other towns outside the danger zone.
President Alberto Fujimori, who had to put off a visit to the stricken Apurimac region due to the rains, warned of further dangers to rescuers and other nearby communities.
"Given the disaster that has already happened, we should avoid another calamity so that those rescuing the corpses are not buried by new landslides," he told reporters at Lima's military airport.
Fujimori wanted to return to the zone to ensure aid for the homeless was being properly administered and not diverted to other people.

The visibly shaken president -- already strained by the 66-day hostage crisis in Lima -- visited the disaster zone on Wednesday. He hugged weeping relatives and sought to encourage rescuers using picks, shovels and their bare hands to pull out mainly mutilated and unrecognizable bodies.
The dangerous rescue work was suspended on Thursday afternoon after rain unleash a fresh mudslide that covered the few roofs of houses still poking out of the mud in Ccocha.
Survivors and the homeless spent a second night in makeshift tents and government shelters. They told harrowing stories of the torrent of mud and rocks that crashed down on them from a mountainside.
Peru's mountain-dwellers have always feared the rainy season's sudden mudslides, which they know by the Quechua Indian word "Huayco."

Jose Saavedra, 40, ran out of the path of the mudslide just before his home was engulfed. "It was all so quick," he said. "I just saw my house collapse with my family and I could not do anything ... The entire population has disappeared."
